column1: What does ISA stand for, and what is its role?
column2: Instruction Set Architecture. It is the contract specifying exactly which bytes a CPU accepts and what they mean — the seam between hardware and software.

What does CISC stand for, and what is its main characteristic?
column2: Complex Instruction Set Computer. Rich, expressive, variable-length instructions (1–15 bytes on x86) that pack more semantics into each instruction.

column1: What does RISC stand for, and what is its main characteristic?
column2: Reduced Instruction Set Computer. Simple, regular, fixed-length instructions (4 bytes) that can be pipelined and clocked faster; the compiler composes complex behaviour from simple parts.

column1: How does a modern x86 chip reconcile a CISC ISA with RISC execution?
column2: It translates CISC instructions into RISC-like µops during decode, then executes those µops in a deeply pipelined, out-of-order RISC core. The ISA stays CISC; the engine inside is RISC.

column1: What is PTX, and how does it differ from SASS?
column2: PTX (Parallel Thread Execution) is NVIDIA’s virtual ISA, compiled from CUDA. SASS is the real hardware ISA. PTX is JIT-compiled to SASS at runtime, allowing programs to run on future GPUs without recompilation.

column1: What is a warp in the GPU ISA context?
column2: A group of 32 threads that execute a single PTX instruction simultaneously, each operating on different data — SIMD-style parallelism.

column1: What is RISC-V, and why is it significant?
column2: An open-source ISA from UC Berkeley that anyone can implement royalty-free. It is small, modern, and modular; most major hyperscalers and AI startups have RISC-V projects underway, often winning quietly in chip controllers and accelerators.
